task.goal: Help first-time visitors use a walk-in neighborhood legal-information desk without making them disclose private details in the waiting area.
hard_constraints: Two volunteers have one desk and printed public information; they do not give legal advice.
No app, registration requirement or public triage of personal cases.
Check successful navigation, waiting confusion and privacy complaints.
task.available_resources: Existing opening hours, printed service scope and a quiet corner.
task.expected_result: An inclusive first-visit flow with escalation to qualified help.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Anonymous turn queue with a private orientation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Make arrival and waiting independent of a visitor’s legal issue. Put a short welcome sheet at the desk stating opening hours, service scope, “legal information, not legal advice,” and “You do not need to explain your situation while waiting.” Visitors take the next numbered paper slip; no name, registration or case description is requested. One volunteer manages turns and explains the process without asking why anyone came. The other offers each visitor a brief orientation in the quiet corner. Visitors can speak, point to printed information or ask the volunteer to read it aloud. They may decline to share details altogether. After orientation, they receive relevant public information or directions to qualified help using referral details already present in the materials. Volunteers explain their limits before discussing any question and do not interpret facts, recommend legal action or predict outcomes. The mechanism is predictable access: visitors secure a place without disclosing a reason, reducing pressure to explain themselves publicly. Implementation needs handwritten slips, a visible current number and consistent volunteer wording. Read numbers aloud and display them so neither hearing nor reading alone is necessary. Assume the quiet corner permits conversation without ordinary waiting-area audibility; inspect this first. If it does not, use it only for general orientation and explain that confidential discussion is unavailable. Limits include slower service when every visitor needs orientation, possible number confusion and referrals constrained by the supplied information.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the prototype with a simple welcome-and-wait instruction in short role-play sessions with first-time users. Ask participants to join the queue, identify their turn, locate service limits and find the route to qualified help without revealing a case. Record unaided completion, questions about waiting and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Use fictional situations only. Reject or revise the design if numbering adds confusion, anyone believes disclosure is required to obtain a turn, or ordinary speech from the corner is intelligible in the waiting area. This checks usability and exposure, not legal outcomes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Visitor-controlled information route
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Let visitors begin with public information independently, with human assistance available by choice. Arrange the existing materials into a short, numbered route: first read the desk’s scope and hours; next browse information; finally choose whether to leave with materials or request a quiet conversation. A plain-language welcome sheet explains that browsing does not require approaching the desk, giving a name or describing a problem. Keep document titles facing the visitor where feasible and do not create separate topic queues or ask people to display their selections. One volunteer offers neutral orientation and reading assistance; the other handles requested conversations in the quiet corner. People requesting conversation receive anonymous turn slips and may wait without holding topic-specific material. A visitor can point privately to a passage instead of narrating personal circumstances. Volunteers explain public information and service boundaries; questions requiring application of law to personal facts are directed to qualified help identified in the available materials. The mechanism is visitor control over whether and when interaction occurs: some first visits can succeed without any case discussion, leaving volunteer time for those needing assistance. Setup requires a one-page route, ordered stacks of existing printouts and a clear place to request assistance. It assumes the materials are understandable enough to support independent use and contain usable referral information. Reading difficulty, limited language coverage and difficulty browsing physically may limit independence, so volunteers must offer assistance without making self-service a prerequisite. Document selection may itself reveal a concern; this approach reduces compelled disclosure but cannot guarantee privacy in a shared room.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the numbered route with the same printouts in an unstructured stack. Give first-time participants fictional goals, including finding opening hours, understanding service limits and reaching qualified help. Include participants who prefer spoken assistance. Observe unaided navigation, uncertainty about whether to wait and privacy concerns about browsing or requesting help. Collect feedback without names or case details. Revise if users mistake browsing for a required step, cannot find human assistance or feel their topic is exposed. A small check can identify failures but cannot establish accessibility across all languages or needs.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Short welcome rounds followed by private individual turns
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Replace repeated public arrival conversations with a brief, recurring explanation of the service. At opening and between individual turns, one volunteer gives a short welcome covering what the desk provides, what volunteers cannot do, how waiting works and how to reach qualified help. Explicitly say that nobody should describe a personal case during the welcome and that attendance is optional. Display the same explanation in print for late arrivals and people who prefer reading. Visitors can join an anonymous numbered queue immediately; missing the welcome never delays access. The second volunteer conducts individual information conversations in the quiet corner. The welcoming volunteer handles only operational questions in the waiting area and redirects attempted personal disclosures gently: “You can keep those details for your individual turn.” Offer individual reading or explanation of the welcome when needed. At the private turn, visitors can request general information without giving personal details. Questions requiring legal judgment receive a clear boundary statement and directions to qualified assistance already listed in the materials. The mechanism is shared expectation-setting: everyone hears the same privacy boundary and waiting instructions before uncertainty prompts a public explanation of their case. It requires a short script, printed equivalent, handwritten turn slips and coordination between two volunteers. Assume brief announcements will not interrupt quiet-corner conversations or expose them; positioning must be checked. Limits include repetitive announcements, language and hearing barriers, and the possibility that a group setting discourages some visitors. Qualified referrals remain dependent on the accuracy and coverage of existing printouts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a fictional arrival exercise comparing the welcome-round format with giving the same explanation separately to each arrival. Include someone arriving halfway through a welcome and someone declining group participation. Check whether participants can identify their next step, understand the wait and locate escalation to qualified help. Count waiting-related clarification requests and invite anonymous privacy complaints. Revise if late arrivals are disadvantaged, anyone thinks attendance is compulsory, personal disclosures occur during the welcome or announcements interfere with private conversations. Treat any apparent improvement as preliminary until checked during ordinary service without collecting case details.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Case-free questions with a direct route to qualified help
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the desk useful without collecting anyone’s personal account. The primary mechanism is information minimization: volunteers help visitors navigate published information, while questions requiring personal facts move to qualified help instead of becoming volunteer case discussions. This reduces dependence on the quiet corner being confidential.

At arrival, display the existing hours and service scope alongside a short instruction: “No name or personal story needed. We can help you find public information and contact details for qualified help.” Offer three neutral requests visitors can say or point to: “Explain this service,” “Help me understand this leaflet,” and “Help me find qualified assistance.” All requests use the same waiting process, so choosing assistance does not create a visible case category. Use anonymous paper turns, with numbers both shown and spoken.

One volunteer handles arrival and waiting questions. The second provides individual assistance in the quiet corner, first explaining that it may not be confidential. Visitors can ask about a published term or passage without describing their circumstances. If someone begins recounting a case, gently interrupt before further details: “You can keep those details private. We can explain the printed information or show you how to contact qualified help.” Volunteers do not reformulate a personal account into a legal question, select a legal strategy or assess urgency from case facts.

Implementation needs a short printed request card, paper turns and rehearsal of the boundary wording. It assumes the existing materials contain current, usable referral details; inspect these first. If they do not, escalation remains an unresolved service gap. Limits include reduced usefulness for visitors unable to separate general questions from their circumstances, possible feelings of rejection, and no guarantee that visitors will avoid spontaneous disclosure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this flow with ordinary private orientation in a small role-play using fictional situations. Ask first-time participants to find information, understand waiting and identify how to reach qualified help. Include someone who starts telling a personal story and someone needing spoken assistance. Record navigation completion, waiting clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Also check whether redirection feels respectful and whether participants mistake public information for advice about their case. Revise or reject if the boundary prevents useful assistance, referral instructions cannot be followed, or personal disclosures remain as frequent as in the comparator. This tests usability and disclosure prevention, not referral availability or legal outcomes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Separate the waiting boundary from the information conversation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use physical separation to keep ordinary service conversations out of the waiting area. The mechanism is controlling where people wait and approach: visitors obtain access without explaining their purpose, and individual assistance begins only after the previous visitor has left the conversation space.

Before adopting this layout, test whether the desk can face the quiet corner while a waiting position elsewhere in the existing space remains outside ordinary conversational hearing. Keep a clear, accessible route between them. If that separation is impossible, this alternative does not work; a quiet corner alone is not evidence of privacy.

Place the existing opening hours and service scope at the waiting boundary, with a plain instruction: “Please wait here. You do not need to explain why you came. A volunteer will welcome you.” One volunteer stays near this boundary, offers spoken or pointing-based assistance and maintains arrival order without names or case categories. The other uses the desk beside the quiet corner for one visitor or visitor-chosen companion group at a time. The welcoming volunteer escorts people who need help reaching their turn; standing in a line is not required.

At the desk, explain that volunteers provide public legal information, not legal advice, and that personal details are optional. Help visitors use the printed materials and locate qualified assistance already listed there. Do not interpret their circumstances or recommend legal action.

Implementation requires repositioning the existing desk and printouts, a paper boundary sign and coordination between the two volunteers. It assumes sufficient accessible space and usable referral information in the materials. Nearby conversations, crowding and companions can still compromise privacy; the layout must not be described as confidential. Missing referral details remain an unresolved escalation gap.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare this layout with waiting immediately beside the desk, using fictional questions and a few first-time participants. Ask visitors to arrive, wait, obtain a leaflet and identify the route to qualified help. Record successful navigation, waiting-related clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints or concerns. Have a participant at the waiting boundary report whether they can understand ordinary-volume conversation at the desk. Reject the layout if speech is intelligible, arrivals routinely cross the boundary prematurely, or visitors needing seating or mobility assistance lose their place. This checks the proposed spatial protection, not confidentiality under every operating condition.

EXPAND.title: Make audibility a condition of service
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the quiet corner’s actual sound separation determine what conversations the desk offers. Before opening, one volunteer speaks fictional sentences at normal conversational volume in the corner while the other listens from the waiting positions. Adjust seating, orientation and speaking volume within the existing space, then repeat. If ordinary speech remains intelligible, offer only general information there and explain that confidential case discussion is unavailable. Do not label a corner private merely because it is quiet.

At entry, a printed instruction gives opening hours, service limits and the next waiting step: “Please wait here; you do not need to explain your situation.” One volunteer handles arrival and turn order without names or topics; the other receives visitors individually in the checked location. Use anonymous paper turns if several people arrive. Offer spoken explanation and reading assistance. Keep waiting visitors away from the conversation position where the available layout permits, without obstructing access or requiring anyone to stand.

At the individual turn, explain the privacy limit before inviting questions. Visitors may request public information without describing circumstances. Volunteers provide printed information and direct questions requiring legal judgment to qualified help listed in it. If waiting-area noise or crowding changes the sound conditions, pause personal discussion, explain the change and return to general information or referral.

The mechanism is environmental exposure control. The strongest prior private-orientation route checks the corner once; this route makes continued conversational service conditional on observable conditions. It needs only both volunteers, existing printouts and usable separation. Its main limits are variable occupancy, accessibility constraints and the possibility that the available room cannot support confidential speech.
EXPAND.experiment: For one opening-period rehearsal, the arrival volunteer owns the audibility check and stop decision. Compare this conditional arrangement with the prior anonymous-queue/private-orientation route using fictional conversations and first-time participants. Check successful navigation through referral, waiting clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints; also record interrupted conversations and extra volunteer minutes. Stop any simulated personal discussion immediately if a waiting listener can repeat its content. Reject the added procedure if it does not reduce exposure or if its interruptions prevent more visitors from reaching information or qualified help than the comparator.

EXPAND.title: Rehearse the referral before the visitor leaves
EXPAND.proposal:
Treat referral as an unfinished navigation task until the visitor can identify a workable next action. Prepare by reviewing only the existing printed materials for qualified-help listings and their stated contact methods, hours, eligibility and costs. Mark missing information as unknown; volunteers must not infer availability or eligibility.

A first-time visitor receives a short printed or spoken welcome: the desk supplies public information, gives no legal advice and needs no name or public case description. One volunteer maintains a simple anonymous turn order and answers operational questions. The other offers an individual turn in the quiet corner, first checking whether speech can be overheard. If confidentiality is unavailable, keep the exchange general. Reading assistance is available throughout.

After providing information, the volunteer asks whether the visitor wants help understanding how to contact qualified assistance. Using the relevant existing listing, walk through the contact action, the service’s stated conditions and any stated alternative. Invite the visitor to point to or describe the next step without explaining their case: “Which contact would you try, and what would you do if it is unavailable?” This is optional and does not become a test for receiving help. If the route is inaccessible, examine another listed route together. If none is usable, explain that limitation plainly; do not promise a successful connection. Visitors can return for navigation assistance without recounting their situation publicly.

The mechanism is detecting referral breakdown before departure. Prior candidates provide directions but do not establish whether visitors can use them. This requires volunteer attention and sufficiently detailed existing listings. It cannot verify current availability, create missing services or substitute for legal advice.
EXPAND.experiment: The information volunteer owns a six-visitor fictional rehearsal comparing referral rehearsal with the prior private-orientation route’s ordinary referral explanation. Include an unavailable first contact and a visitor who prefers spoken assistance. Check whether participants reach a supported next step, understand waiting and report privacy concerns; record added minutes and whether the rehearsal feels pressuring. Stop if volunteers invent missing referral facts or elicit case details to establish understanding. Drop the extra step if it produces no navigation improvement after accounting for time and discomfort. Actual access to qualified help remains unproven by this rehearsal.

EXPAND.title: Calibrate volunteers’ explain-or-hand-off decisions
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a short paired practice before opening to reduce inconsistent decisions about what volunteers may explain. With the printed service scope in front of them, the two volunteers independently sort fictional requests into three actions: explain public information, clarify the information requested without soliciting personal facts, or direct the visitor to qualified help. Each explains the choice by pointing to the scope or printed material. Where the scope leaves uncertainty, use the conservative handoff boundary and acknowledge the uncertainty. Neither volunteer serves as a legal authority for the other.

Practice a close pair: “Where does this leaflet describe the response deadline?” permits locating and reading the passage; “Given when I received these papers, what is my deadline?” requires applying law to facts and goes to qualified help. Add an unfamiliar request, such as whether signing an agreement could affect immigration status, to check that an unfamiliar topic does not invite speculation. Also practice stopping an unsolicited public case account with a neutral invitation to keep details for an individual turn.

During service, one volunteer welcomes visitors, explains anonymous waiting and offers reading assistance. The other handles individual questions in the quiet corner after explaining its privacy limits. Nobody must disclose a case to join the queue. Volunteers use the practiced distinction, provide the relevant printout where appropriate and explain how to approach qualified help using listed referral details. If a volunteer realizes they have crossed the boundary, they promptly withdraw the interpretation and redirect the question without repeating personal details publicly.

The mechanism is more consistent staff judgment, rather than another arrival format. It uses existing scope documents, fictional prompts and a brief preparation period. Limits include ambiguous scope, inadequate referral listings and over-referral that unnecessarily withholds useful general information.
EXPAND.experiment: One volunteer administers a brief rehearsal; both independently answer the close pair and unfamiliar case before discussing them. Then compare simulated first visits under this calibrated approach with the prior private-orientation route using its boundary statement alone. Check successful navigation to information or qualified help, waiting confusion and anonymous privacy complaints. Record preparation time, unnecessary handoffs and any unsupported interpretation. Stop on any legal-advice response or prompted public disclosure. Revise or abandon the practice if decisions remain inconsistent, or if extra handoffs reduce useful access without improving privacy or scope compliance. Agreement between volunteers alone does not establish legal correctness.

EXPAND.title: Anonymous turn queue with private orientation — improvement: recover from an unfinished wait
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve the anonymous queue’s direct benefit: visitors obtain a turn without explaining their problem. Add an executable response when closing, interruption or an unexpectedly long conversation prevents the queue from finishing. The source already checks audibility and offers accessible orientation; the change addresses visitors leaving with only an unfulfilled number.

Display existing hours, service scope and a short instruction: “Take a number; no name or case description needed. You can request general information or referral directions while waiting.” Use handwritten slips and show and announce turns. One volunteer handles arrival and operational assistance; the other provides individual orientation in the quiet corner. Check audibility before using it; if ordinary speech carries, restrict exchanges to general information and explain the limitation. Offer reading assistance and pointing to materials.

The arrival volunteer monitors remaining opening time without promising service times. When another individual turn cannot reasonably be offered, stop issuing numbers and explain this promptly to anyone still waiting. Offer existing general information and qualified-help contact directions immediately, or the next published opening time. Visitors need not explain why waiting is unsuitable. If someone mentions a deadline, do not calculate it or suggest that returning later is safe; offer listed qualified-help directions immediately and state that availability is unconfirmed.

Volunteers remain responsible for explaining these options until departure; providing a listing does not mean another service has accepted responsibility. If orientation is interrupted, retain the visitor’s anonymous place and resume before calling another number.

This requires paper, a writing implement and coordination within existing hours. It cannot create referral capacity or determine legal urgency. Giving waiting visitors assistance may slow individual turns, so that displaced workload must be measured.
EXPAND.experiment: The arrival volunteer owns two short, matched rehearsals comparing this revision with the source queue’s ordinary operation. Use fictional arrivals, an interrupted turn and a queue that exceeds closing time. Check successful navigation to information or a supported referral action, waiting clarification requests and anonymous privacy complaints. Also count unfinished departures, volunteer minutes and delays imposed on other visitors. Stop if anyone is encouraged to postpone a possible deadline, asked publicly for case details or promised an unconfirmed referral. Keep the added recovery step only if it reduces stranded departures without a comparable loss of access elsewhere; otherwise shorten the recovery explanation and retest.

EXPAND.title: Visitor-held written questions as an optional communication channel
EXPAND.proposal:
Let visitors communicate a question silently during their individual turn, reducing reliance on speech that may carry into the waiting area. Unlike browsing or pointing to a leaflet, this allows a visitor to express a question absent from the printed materials without saying it aloud.

At entry, display hours, service limits and anonymous waiting instructions. State that visitors may speak, point or bring a written question; writing is optional and never secures priority. One volunteer manages numbered turns and offers neutral orientation. The other receives visitors individually in the quiet corner. Neither asks for a name or publicly asks what the question concerns.

Offer the blank reverse of a service-scope sheet and an ordinary pencil, if available. Suggest a general question without names, addresses or identifying documents. Visitors may write during their individual turn if waiting-area sightlines would expose the page. They retain the sheet, hand it directly to the information volunteer and take it back afterward; volunteers make no copy or case record. Do not provide unattended collection trays.

The volunteer reads silently, locates applicable public information and lets the visitor point to passages. Explain aloud only general material when audibility is uncertain. Questions requiring application of law to personal circumstances go to qualified help using existing listings. The visitor chooses whether to write a further question, use another communication method or stop. If interrupted, return the page immediately and preserve the visitor’s turn. If a listed contact is unusable, examine another existing listing; acknowledge when none is available. Never imply that waiting for this desk protects a deadline.

This needs spare printable space and a pencil; without them, retain spoken general orientation and pointing assistance. It may help some visitors but burden others, and visible handwriting can itself expose information. It offers no guarantee of confidentiality.
EXPAND.experiment: The information volunteer owns a six-visit fictional rehearsal comparing optional visitor-held writing with ordinary spoken individual orientation. Include a visitor who prefers writing, one who cannot comfortably write and an interrupted exchange. Check successful navigation to information or qualified-help directions, waiting confusion and anonymous privacy complaints. Record total service time, reading difficulty and whether a waiting observer can see or hear question content. Stop on a retained page, compelled writing, exposed content or unsupported legal interpretation. Withdraw the writing option if exposure or extra delays outweigh any observed improvement; preserve anonymous access and other communication choices.
